I'm Rekha, and last winter I matched with someone called Nikhil on a dating app. Architect, dog lover, perfect grammar. Within a week he was saying he had never felt this way.
My friend Sonali had drilled three rules into me after her cousin lost savings to a fake profile: video call early, check the photos, never send money or private pictures to someone you haven't met.
So on day eight I said, "Quick video call tonight? Five minutes." He said his camera was broken. While we chatted, I ran his photos through a reverse image search. They belonged to a travel blogger in Portugal.
I didn't accuse him. I just said, "I'd love to keep talking, but only after a live call." The replies turned sharp: "You don't trust me? After everything?" Then he unmatched.
I reported the profile. It stung for a day. Then I felt proud. A real person would simply have turned on the camera.

qa.q: Whose photos did the reverse image search find?
qa.a: The photos belonged to a travel blogger in Portugal.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after Nikhil unmatched?
qa.a: It stung for a day, and then Rekha felt proud for sticking to the checks.

qa.q: Which check revealed the most, and why?
qa.a: The reverse image search showed the photos were someone else's, and the calm request for a live call drew out anger instead of acceptance, which a real person would not show.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel hearing Rekha's story?
qa.a: Sonali would likely feel relieved and glad the rules helped, especially after seeing a cousin lose savings to a fake profile.

grounding: A person insists on an early live video call, reverse-searches the photos and refuses to send money or pictures, and the fake match reacts with anger.

The mobile tower on the water tank gave Kamal two bars if he stood by the fertiliser sacks, so that was where he read Rhea's messages every night.
Four months of good-mornings. Voice notes in a soft accent from abroad. She called him her gentle farmer.
Tonight the message was different. "Kamal, I'm in hospital after an accident, my cards are blocked. I need 60,000 by morning or they won't treat me. I have no one else."
His hands went cold. He pictured her alone and hurt. The money in the shop account was meant for the monsoon stock. He sent it anyway, at 1 a.m., before he could think.
By morning her number no longer existed.
When Manjula Bhabhi asked at breakfast why he looked ill, he said it was the heat. He couldn't say it aloud, that the gentle voice had never been real. So he reported nothing, and the silence sat on him all day.

qa.a: He stood by the fertiliser sacks, where the tower gave two bars.

qa.a: He felt cold with fear for her, picturing her alone and hurt, which pushed him to act before thinking.

qa.a: He could tell Manjula Bhabhi, report the fraud quickly to the cybercrime helpline and his bank, and remember that being fooled by professionals is not a personal failure.

They had talked every day for five months. She knew his mother's name, his favourite dumplings, the song he sang badly. She had been saving to fly to him. Now, two hours before the flight, this.
Chen opened his banking app. His student loan had just come in. His thumb hovered. If he didn't pay, she'd be alone and scared. If he didn't pay, maybe she'd think he didn't love her.
A small voice asked: why can't she video call from the airport?
He typed, "Video call me, just ten seconds." The reply came instantly: "No time!! Do you want me or not?"
Chen stared at the screen, heart pounding, no longer sure whether this was love or fear.

I'm Dhruv. Last year someone I'd been talking to online for two months, "Maya", asked me to buy gift cards worth fifteen thousand. Her mother was in hospital; she'd pay me back Friday.
I liked Maya a lot. I still felt the tug. But after reading about scams, I had made myself one rule: if someone I've never met asks for money in any form, gift cards, crypto, a transfer, that's a stop sign. Not a maybe. A stop.
So I stopped. I didn't argue with her. I called Chaitanya, who has known me since school, and read him the messages. He didn't laugh. He said, "Good that you called. Let's report it."
We reported the profile to the app, and I filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal. It took twenty minutes.
The embarrassing part was admitting I'd fallen for the chat at all. Chaitanya said the people who run these scams do it for a living. That helped.

It was Gargi's fourth visit to the Aizawl branch that month, and Lalremsiami, at the counter, recognised the account number on the transfer slip before she looked up.
"Same beneficiary?" she asked.
Gargi nodded, cheeks pink. "His business account is frozen. It's just until Friday."
Lalremsiami didn't scold. She lowered her voice. "Can I ask a few things, just between us? Have you met him in person?"
"Not yet. He's in Malta."
"Has he ever video called?"
"His camera..." Gargi trailed off.
Lalremsiami had seen this story in the bank's fraud training: the same charming engineer, the same frozen account, scripts shared by organised groups who do this all day. Gargi wasn't foolish. Gargi was up against professionals.
"Would you sit with our fraud officer for ten minutes before sending? No pressure. I'll come too."
Gargi looked at the slip for a long moment, then nodded.

Gopika had applied to thirty-one jobs since graduating and heard back from none. So when the message came while she stood in the ration shop queue, she read it three times.
"Congratulations! Selected for work-from-home data entry. Rs 38,000 per month, 2 hours daily. Pay Rs 1,999 registration to confirm your seat. Offer valid 1 hour."
She thought of Appa's cough, the loan on the tractor, her younger brother Tejas's school fees. Two hours a day. She could do that between chores.
She paid from the money kept for her exam forms.
The next message asked for her bank login "to set up salary". Then a security deposit of Rs 5,000. Gopika sat on the temple steps, the phone warm in her hand, and felt her stomach turn. The hurry, the fees, a salary that needed her password.
She didn't send more. But she couldn't make herself tell Amma about the 1,999, not yet.

qa.a: It would look more like a real employer, since real jobs don't charge to hire or ask for passwords, and Gopika could check it calmly.

I'm Deepak. Last spring an agent in our town offered me a hotel job abroad, with just Rs 60,000 for processing and my passport to keep "for safety".
My cousin had gone abroad through an agent and come home with nothing, so I did three things before saying yes to anything.
First, I checked whether the agency was on the government's list of registered recruiting agents. It wasn't. Second, I wrote to the hotel through its official website. They replied that they hire only through their own careers page and never charge fees. Third, I asked my friend Gargi, who works in HR in Pune, to read the offer letter. She laughed and said, "Deepak, the logo is blurry."
I didn't pay. I didn't hand over my passport. I told the agent no and reported him to the local police.
Six months later I got a real job in Pune, through a real interview, without paying anyone a rupee.

passage:
I'm Sumit. For six weeks last year, I lied every evening at dinner.
I had put my savings, three years of them, into a trading app a friend of a friend swore by. When it froze, a "recovery agent" called and said I could get it back for a fee. I paid that too. Chasing it felt better than admitting it was gone.
At home, Ma asked about my savings once, and I changed the subject so fast she looked at me strangely. I stopped sleeping. I kept refreshing the dead app as if it might wake up.
Wasim noticed first. He cornered me on the office terrace: "You look like someone died." I told him everything and waited for him to call me stupid. He said, "Okay. Today we report it."
We filed complaints on the cybercrime portal and with the regulator that evening. That night I told Ma and Papa. Ma cried. Then she made tea.

qa.q: How long did Sumit lie at dinner?
qa.a: Sumit lied every evening at dinner for six weeks.

qa.q: Why did chasing the loss feel better to Sumit than admitting it?
qa.a: Admitting it meant facing shame and the family's reaction, so paying the recovery fee kept alive a hope that the money wasn't gone.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Telling Wasim everything on the terrace led to reporting that same evening and telling Ma and Papa, which ended the hiding and gave the best chance to limit the damage.

qa.q: What might Ma have felt when she was finally told?
qa.a: Ma likely felt shock and sadness, which is why she cried, but also relief at the truth, shown when she made tea.

grounding: A person who lost savings to a fake scheme hides it out of shame and even pays a recovery fee, until Wasim helps report it and tell the family.

passage:
Branch officer's note, 18 July. Mridul.
Kashish, a customer I know from her salary account, came in asking to break her fixed deposit early, today, in cash. Her hands were shaking and she kept checking her phone.
I asked gently whether everything was all right. After a while she told me: three weeks ago she lost most of her savings in an online investment club. Someone from the club now promised to recover it if she paid a release fee. She had not told her husband. "He'll think I'm an idiot," she said.
I told her the recovery offer is a common second trap, that she is not an idiot, and that reporting early matters.
Outcome today: she decided not to break the deposit. I sat with her while she called the cybercrime helpline and flagged the transactions with our fraud team. She plans to tell her husband tonight, with her sister present.

qa.q: What did Kashish ask to do at the branch?
qa.a: She asked to break her fixed deposit early, today, in cash.

qa.q: What was Kashish afraid of?
qa.a: She was afraid her husband would think she was an idiot, which is why she had hidden the loss.

qa.q: What steps did Mridul take to limit the damage?
qa.a: Mridul explained the recovery offer was a second trap, said she was not an idiot, and sat with her while she called the cybercrime helpline and flagged the transactions with the fraud team.

qa.q: How might Kashish's husband react when told tonight, with her sister present?
qa.a: He may be shocked or upset at first, but hearing it early and with support gives them a better chance to face it together.

grounding: A bank officer notices a woman's distress, learns she hid an investment loss from her husband and is being offered a fake recovery, and helps her report it.
